title: Who Can Log In?
story: Audit season has arrived, along with an auditor whose first question is which accounts can open an interactive shell. The answer is somewhere in /etc/passwd, between the service accounts and a chat bot with an unfortunate name.
objective: Print only the names of the accounts in /etc/passwd whose login shell is /bin/bash, one name per line.
hints: Each /etc/passwd line is one account split into seven colon-separated fields. The account name comes first and the login shell comes last.
grep matches anywhere on a line, so anchor the shell to the end with $. cut -d: -f1 then keeps only the first colon-separated field.
explanation: Many system files are delimited records. cut -d: -f1 selects the name field from /etc/passwd, and anchoring the pattern to the end of the line makes grep test the shell field instead of any text that merely mentions bash, such as a home directory. Selecting fields first with cut -d: -f1,7 and filtering afterward is an equally valid route.

files.content:
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
www-data:x:33:33:www-data:/var/www:/usr/sbin/nologin
postgres:x:112:120:PostgreSQL administrator:/var/lib/postgresql:/bin/false
deploy:x:1001:1001:Release automation:/home/deploy:/bin/bash
bashbot:x:1002:1002:Chat bot:/opt/bashbot:/usr/sbin/nologin
oncall:x:1003:1003:On-call engineer:/home/oncall:/bin/bash
